extracted.intended_audience: medical journal editors, peer reviewers, and researchers interested in peer review policy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and arguments about moving from closed to open peer review in medical journals, including specific implementation steps, ethical rationale, evidence from trials, and anticipated benefits and harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify reviewers to authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ will identify to authors the names of those who have reviewed their papers, including the names of in house editorial and statistical advisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the first step toward openness: authors will know who reviewed their work. It is presented as an immediate policy change applicable to all new papers under review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full public transparency of the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Open up the whole system so that anybody interested can see the whole process on the world wide web.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible further steps include listing reviewers at the end of articles and moving to a system where authors and readers can watch the peer review system on the web as it happens and contribute their comments. The goal is to make peer review an increasingly scientific discourse rather than a summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical imperative for openness (accountability)
rubrics_metrics.description: It seems wrong for somebody making an important judgment on the work of others to do so in secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying reviewers links ‘privilege and duty’ and reminds reviewers that with power comes responsibility; openness is argued from an ethical standpoint to reduce arbitrary or destructive judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness links accountability with credit for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness links accountability with credit: reviewers should receive academic credit for their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One defect of closed review is that reviewers don’t receive academic credit; publishing reviewer names would allow credit to be attributed and recognised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness should reduce abusive behaviour and misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness should eliminate some of the worst abuses of peer review, where reviewers—under the cloak of anonymity—steal ideas or procrastinate, and should reduce curt, abusive, destructive reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors have observed abusive reviews that would likely not have been written if the reviewer were identifiable; transparency is presented as a deterrent to such behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk: openness may deter junior reviewers (fear of reprisals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Junior reviewers will be reluctant to criticise the work of senior researchers for fear of reprisals; this fear is particularly acute for researchers whose livelihoods depend on winning grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editorial recognises this trade-off and notes that junior reviewers (those under 40) have repeatedly been shown to give the best opinions; the policy allows reviewers to decline to review if they do not want to be identified and hopes cultural change will reduce fear of reprisals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow reviewers to decline if unwilling to be identified
rubrics_metrics.description: A few reviewers have said that they don’t want to review if they will be identified, and anyone can decline to review a particular paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical accommodation to address reviewer reluctance: identification is not enforced if the reviewer chooses not to participate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement changes incrementally and research effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ will introduce open review and 'research as we go'—evaluating impact and likely expanding transparency based on evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy change should be guided by trials and evidence; the BMJ cites randomised trials (including its own) and plans to monitor effects of openness as it extends practices (e.g., naming reviewers publicly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use evidence from trials to evaluate peer review models
rubrics_metrics.description: Randomised controlled trials have examined blinding and open review; one BMJ trial found open review does not lead to higher quality opinions, nor to poorer quality ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions should be evidence-based: prior trials of blinding/unmasking have mixed results, and the BMJ uses this evidence to justify implementing open review largely for ethical reasons despite no observed change in review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise known defects of traditional peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is slow, expensive, profligate of academic time, highly subjective, prone to bias, easily abused, poor at detecting gross defects, and almost useless for detecting fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These deficiencies (supported by cited literature) are the problems openness and other reforms aim to address; assessing any peer review system should account for these limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary benefit: peer review improves published work rather than perfectly sorting quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is probably more useful for improving what is eventually published than for sorting the wheat from the chaff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating peer review systems, consider their role in improving manuscripts and published science, not only in gatekeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural change as a goal to protect junior reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: By moving to open review the BMJ hopes to contribute to a broader culture change so that junior researchers cease to fear reprisals from senior ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openness is presented not only as a policy but as part of a cultural strategy to make criticizing senior researchers safer over time; this is offered as mitigation for the risk of losing candid junior reviewers.
